topic: diagnosing an incorrect centre, vector or scale factor

traps.desc: subtracted the image coordinate from the original instead of the other way round

problems.desc: Part (c), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says a translation vector runs from the original point to the image, so each component is the image coordinate minus the original coordinate, and that ana reversed that subtraction, which flips the sign of both components and sends the point the wrong way. Half credit if it gives the correct subtraction order without saying what the reversal does to the direction. No credit for correcting the numbers with no account of the error.

traps.desc: added the scale factor to each coordinate instead of multiplying
added the scale factor to the second coordinate instead of multiplying

problems.desc: Part (b), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says a dilation multiplies each coordinate by the scale factor rather than adding it, that adding a fixed amount to both coordinates is a translation, and that ben therefore performed a slide instead of an enlargement, so his image is the same size as the original. Half credit if it gives the multiplying rule without naming the move he actually carried out. No credit for redoing the arithmetic with no diagnosis.

traps.desc: subtracted the two sides instead of dividing

problems.desc: Part (b), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says a scale factor answers how many times as long, which makes it a quotient of matching sides rather than their difference, and that cara computed a difference; it should note that a difference carries a unit of length while a scale factor is a pure number. Half credit if it gives the division without explaining why a difference cannot be a scale factor. No credit for stating the correct value alone.

traps.desc: dilated about the origin instead of the given centre
dilated the second coordinate about the origin instead of the given centre

problems.desc: Part (b), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says the centre of a dilation is the one point that does not move, so the scaling must be applied to each coordinate's offset from that centre and then added back, and that using the origin scaled the wrong offsets, giving an image of the right size in the wrong place. Half credit if it states the centre form of the rule without saying what goes wrong when the origin is used. No credit for recomputing with no diagnosis.

traps.desc: used the area ratio itself as the linear scale factor

problems.desc: Part (b), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says areas of similar figures scale by the square of the linear factor, so the ratio handed over is already the factor squared and a square root is needed before it can be used as a length ratio; it should note that the reported value would only be right if area scaled the same way length does. Half credit if it names the square-root step without explaining why the given ratio is the square. No credit for stating the correct value alone.

traps.desc: dilated about the origin instead of about the endpoint given as the centre

problems.slot: (b) length of the correct image segment

problems.desc: Part (c), instructor-judged. Full credit: the response says both images have length 12 because a dilation multiplies every length by the scale factor whatever centre is used, but the centre fixes where the image lands, and dilating about the origin moved the segment away from the endpoint that was supposed to stay put. Half credit if it says the lengths agree without explaining what the centre controls. No credit for claiming the student's answer is entirely correct or entirely wrong.
